study_identification.title: Structural variability of the cerebral cortex in schizophrenia and its association with clinical symptoms

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate regional and global structural variability of the cerebral cortex in patients with schizophrenia compared to healthy controls using coefficient of variation (CV) and person-based similarity index (PBSI) scores, and to examine associations between structural variability and clinical symptoms, particularly cognitive functions.

model_origin.reason: This study does not use traditional normative modeling. Instead, it uses the Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI) approach, which quantifies within-group similarity of cortical structural profiles. The PBSI score is calculated within the same diagnostic group by correlating each individual's cortical profile with all other individuals in that group. This is fundamentally different from normative modeling, which typically builds a model from healthy controls to predict deviations in patients. The question about model origin (New vs Pre-trained) is not applicable to this methodological approach.
model_origin.supporting_text: We calculated the PBSI scores to estimate the global variation in cortical measures within the same group. Following a procedure validated in previous studies (Antoniades et al., 2021; Doucet et al., 2019, 2020a, 2020b; Janssen et al., 2021), the PBSI score for the cortical measure was calculated within the same group. First, for each cortical measure, we concatenated the measurements of the 308 cortical structures into a single vector to generate a person-specific profile of cortical measures across the 308 cortical structures. In each group, the cortical structural profile of an individual correlated with the respective profiles of all other individuals within the same group using the Spearman's correlation coefficient rho. This process yielded n-1 correlation coefficients per participant, where n is the number of participants in the same group. The correlation coefficients were then averaged to generate the PBSI score for the cortical measures.
model_origin.location: Main paper, Methods section, Global variability of cortical measures subsection (page 3)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Spearman's correlation was used to test associations between PBSI scores and clinical variables (illness duration, PANSS scores, neurocognitive test results including IQ, CTT-1, and word fluency). For illness duration associations, age effects were regressed out. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare clinical variables between 'deviant' patients (PBSI z-score < mean - 1.5 SD relative to HC distribution) and 'other patients'. Group comparisons were also performed between patients with severe symptoms/poor cognitive function (upper 10th percentile for PANSS; below mean - 2 SD for cognition) versus other patients. Bonferroni correction was applied for multiple testing across all tests considering measurement tools and study groups. Results showed significant positive correlations between PBSI-GV and PBSI-All scores with full-scale IQ (PBSI-GV: rho=0.256, Bonferroni-corrected p=0.001; PBSI-All: rho=0.242, Bonferroni-corrected p=0.001). Deviant patients with lower PBSI-GV and PBSI-All scores had significantly lower IQ scores than other patients (PBSI-GV: W=2956.5, Bonferroni-corrected p<0.001; PBSI-All: W=2968.5, Bonferroni-corrected p=0.046).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Patients with schizophrenia showed greater regional and global structural variability than healthy controls, with lower PBSI scores across all cortical measures and higher CV in select regions, and patients with markedly deviant PBSI scores for gray matter volume and combined measures exhibited significantly lower general intelligence.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Regional variability: Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly higher CV for surface area in the left insula and right precentral region, and for cortical thickness in left precuneus, posterior cingulate, right isthmus cingulate, posterior cingulate, and superior parietal cortex. Global variability: All PBSI scores were significantly lower in SCZ compared to HC (PBSI-SA: HC 0.383±0.044 vs SCZ 0.365±0.047, p<0.001; PBSI-GV: HC 0.598±0.041 vs SCZ 0.574±0.043, p<0.001; PBSI-CT: HC 0.682±0.039 vs SCZ 0.660±0.040, p<0.001; PBSI-LGI: HC 0.919±0.013 vs SCZ 0.910±0.017, p<0.001; PBSI-All: HC 0.650±0.028 vs SCZ 0.632±0.030, p<0.001). Lower PBSI scores were also observed in most Yeo and von Economo subnetworks. PBSI-GV and PBSI-All scores showed positive correlations with PANSS-positive scores (rho=0.109 and 0.110, p=0.044 and 0.039 after Bonferroni correction). Clinical associations: In patients, PBSI-GV and PBSI-All scores positively correlated with full-scale IQ (PBSI-GV: rho=0.256, p=0.001; PBSI-All: rho=0.242, p=0.001 after Bonferroni correction). Patients with deviant PBSI-GV and PBSI-All scores (<mean-1.5 SD) had significantly lower IQ than other patients (Bonferroni-corrected p<0.001 and p=0.046). Patients with IQ <mean-2 SD had lower PBSI-SA, PBSI-GV, and PBSI-All scores than other patients (Bonferroni-corrected p=0.024, 0.015, and 0.004). No significant associations were found between PBSI scores and illness duration or daily olanzapine equivalents after correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, the significant associations between PBSI-GV, PBSI-All, and IQ scores were derived from a small subset of patients for whom IQ scores were available (n=267 for IQ, 191 for CTT-1, 138 for word fluency), not the entire population (n=695). Second, morphometric measure variations derived from different sample characteristics in terms of race, cognitive function, and education were not considered in the ComBat harmonization process; previous studies reported relationships between cortical thickness and ethnicity, general intelligence, education, and socioeconomic status. Third, despite ComBat harmonization reducing site differences, some significant group differences in mean cortical measures remained. Fourth, cumulative exposure to antipsychotic medications was not considered, though associations between cortical/subcortical morphometric measures and antipsychotics have been reported; antipsychotic medications may contribute to greater heterogeneity. Fifth, a comprehensive assessment of cognitive impairment (e.g., MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery) was not available; only limited cognitive tests were used. Sixth, the cross-sectional design limits interpretation of negative associations between PBSI scores and illness duration; longitudinal studies are needed. Seventh, the study population may not be representative of the full range of schizophrenia patients as individual studies required informed consent and tended to include patients with relatively stable clinical symptoms. Eighth, the significant group differences in contribution effects were observed for many cortical regions (113-169 regions depending on measure), differing from previous studies, possibly due to larger sample size and finer cortical parcellation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates the utility of PBSI scores to identify a subset of schizophrenia patients with marked deviations in cortical structural similarity who exhibit lower general intelligence. The authors note that their findings provide neurobiological evidence partially accounting for the heterogeneity of schizophrenia observed in clinical practice, particularly regarding general intelligence. They suggest that future studies focusing on personalized medicine are needed to individualize diagnosis and treatment of schizophrenia, and that identification of neurobiological biomarkers may contribute to individualized diagnostic and treatment plans. The PBSI approach extends beyond traditional case-control designs by accounting for individual-level variation within diagnostic groups. The study used a normative modeling framework to classify patients as 'deviant' (z-score < mean - 1.5 SD) versus 'other patients' based on HC distribution, demonstrating clinical utility of this approach. Bootstrap resampling showed PBSI scores were robust to the number of included cortical regions (plateauing at ~100 regions). The study also calculated PBSI scores for functional subnetworks (Yeo atlas) and cytoarchitectonic subnetworks (von Economo atlas), showing widespread reductions in SCZ across multiple brain systems. This study is notable for using a finer cortical parcellation (308 regions) than atlas-based schemes and including local gyrification index alongside conventional measures.

general_notes.general_notes: IMPORTANT METHODOLOGICAL NOTE: This study does NOT use traditional normative modeling in the sense of building a model from healthy controls to predict individual deviations. Instead, it uses the Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI), which quantifies within-group similarity of cortical structural profiles. PBSI scores are calculated separately within HC and SCZ groups by correlating each individual's profile with all others in the same group. This is a similarity-based approach to measuring heterogeneity, not a predictive normative model. The study does employ a 'normative modeling framework' in one analysis where patient PBSI scores are converted to z-scores using HC mean and SD to identify 'deviant' patients, but this is a secondary application. The primary methodology is variability/similarity analysis using CV and PBSI metrics. Scanner information: Seven different sites/scanners were used: AMC (3T Philips Achieva), JNUH (3T Siemens Verio), COBRE (3T Siemens Trio), NMorphCH (scanner NA, 32-channel head coil), MCIC (3T Siemens Trio, 8-channel head coil), fBIRN (scanner NA), UCLA (3T Siemens Trio). Detailed acquisition parameters are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Data aggregation approach: The study pooled data from seven datasets, performed ComBat harmonization with age, sex, and diagnosis as covariates, applied systematic QC (outlier exclusion based on mean±3.5 SD across 1232 measures), and conducted age/sex matching (subsampling in fBIRN and UCLA datasets using MatchIt). Initial sample included 540 HC and 754 SCZ; final analyzed sample was 420 HC and 695 SCZ. Cortical parcellation: Used a 308-region parcellation derived from the Desikan-Killiany atlas, providing finer granularity than standard atlas-based schemes. Rationale: better topological properties of cortical network. Four measures per region: surface area, gray matter volume, cortical thickness, and local gyrification index (total 1232 measures per participant). Local gyrification index was included because it is less affected by age, disease processes, and psychotropic drugs than gray matter volume. Subnetwork analyses: PBSI scores were calculated for subnetworks defined by the Yeo atlas (7 resting-state networks) and von Economo atlas (cytoarchitectonic parcellation). Most subnetworks showed lower PBSI scores in SCZ except for select network/measure combinations. Robustness analyses: Bootstrap resampling with randomly selected subsets of regions (20-300 in increments of 20, 100 repetitions each) showed PBSI scores plateau at ~100 regions. Leave-one-out analyses assessed contribution of each regional measure to PBSI scores, revealing significant group differences in contributions for 73-169 regions depending on measure. Clinical data availability: Information on illness duration (n=610 patients), PANSS scores (n=681), IQ (n=267, from AMC, COBRE, and 62 from JNUH), word fluency (n=138, from COBRE only), and CTT-1 (n=191, from AMC and COBRE) was available for subsets of participants. Medication data: Daily olanzapine equivalents available for subsets from AMC, COBRE, and UCLA. Most patients received atypical antipsychotics. SAPS/SANS scores from NMorphCH, MCIC, fBIRN, and UCLA were converted to PANSS positive and negative scores using validated equations. Study conducted 2021-2023 based on IRB approval date (IRB No. 2021-0423, Asan Medical Center). The study acknowledges the Japanese research funding (NRF-2021R1F1A11057227 for SWJ; HR18C0016 for YCC). Published 2023 in Psychological Medicine with open access license. This appears to be one of the larger PBSI studies in schizophrenia, with 695 patients compared to previous studies (Antoniades et al. 2021 with first-episode psychosis; Doucet et al. 2020b; Janssen et al. 2021).
